summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces a theoretical and experimental framework for three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics, overcoming the limitations of previous two-dimensional (2D) systems that suffered from out-of-plane losses and planar confinement. The authors develop a 3D photonic crystal with a complete photonic bandgap, utilizing a diamond-like lattice structure composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods. Unlike 2D valley photonic crystals (VPCs) which feature a single pair of valleys with scalar valley Chern numbers, the proposed 3D system exhibits triple pairs of valleys characterized by vectorial valley Chern numbers (VCVs). This vectorial nature enables the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The study demonstrates that the direction of these surface states is intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule relative to the VCVs. Experimentally, the authors verify the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature using a pump-probe measurement with a vectorial chiral source array, selectively exciting chiral Bloch modes. They further demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a specifically shaped sample, showing that these states propagate diffractionlessly and can navigate sharp corners without intervalley scattering. The findings highlight the potential of 3D valley photonics for applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, offering a pathway to manipulate electromagnetic waves with full 3D confinement and control.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a theoretical and experimental framework for three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics, overcoming the limitations of previous two-dimensional (2D) systems that suffered from out-of-plane losses and planar confinement. The authors develop a 3D photonic crystal with a complete photonic bandgap, utilizing a diamond-like lattice structure composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods. Unlike 2D valley photonic crystals (VPCs) which feature a single pair of valleys with scalar valley Chern numbers, the proposed 3D system exhibits triple pairs of valleys characterized by vectorial valley Chern numbers (VCVs). This vectorial nature enables the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The study demonstrates that the direction of these surface states is intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule relative to the VCVs. Experimentally, the authors verify the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature using a pump-probe measurement with a vectorial chiral source array, selectively exciting chiral Bloch modes. They further demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a specifically shaped sample, showing that these states propagate diffractionlessly and can navigate sharp corners without intervalley scattering. The findings highlight the potential of 3D valley photonics for applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, offering a pathway to manipulate electromagnetic waves with full 3D confinement and control.

Research Context
Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to manipulate electromagnetic waves. Current valley photonics has been limited to two dimensions, suffering from out-of-plane losses. Two-dimensional valley photonic crystals typically contain a single pair of valleys. Previous 2D systems can only manipulate the flow of light in planar geometries. Full confinement of light requires a complete photonic bandgap. Achieving a complete photonic bandgap remains a significant challenge.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a framework of 3D topological valley photonics. The 3D framework goes beyond the binary valley degree of freedom. The 3D model involves triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D BZ. These pairs are differentiated by band geometric quantities along distinct directions. The study introduces a vectorial valley-contrasting physics perspective. The hypothesis is that valley Chern vectors govern the propagation direction. The authors predict the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices. They also predict canalized chiral valley surface states.

Methodological Details
The study uses a 3D photonic crystal with lattice constant a = 20 mm. The lattice vectors are defined as a1, a2, and a3. The structure is a photonic diamond with nearest-neighbor and next-nearest neighbor couplings. Carbon atoms and bonds are replaced by PEC spheres and rods. Each fcc cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2. Nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm. The next-nearest coupling suppresses high-order modes for a clean bandstructure. The band structure is analyzed for cases where ∆D = 0 and ∆D ≠ 0. When ∆D = 0, inversion symmetry is preserved, hosting nodal lines. When ∆D ≠ 0, inversion symmetry is broken, forming a complete photonic bandgap. The 3D gapped phase has six valleys at Wα±. The effective Hamiltonian is derived using the k · p method. The mass term m is induced by breaking inversion symmetry. A vectorial chiral source array is used for selective excitation. The source array consists of four sources with specific relative positions. Relative phase delays are set to form clockwise or counterclockwise phase winding. The boundary condition is modified by covering the surface with a metallic plate. The diameter of the outmost metallic sphere D3 and distance h are tuned. The specific boundary condition is satisfied when h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm.

Procedures And Architectures
The 3D photonic crystal is fabricated with a diamond-like lattice. PEC spheres and rods form the structural elements of the crystal. The band structure is calculated for different sphere diameter differences. Nodal lines are identified when inversion symmetry is preserved. A complete photonic bandgap is formed when inversion symmetry is broken. The Berry curvature is calculated to verify vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The valley Chern vector (VCV) is calculated by integrating Berry curvature. The VCVs are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). A metallic plate is used to modify the boundary condition. The plate features perforations for inserting the source and probe. The hole interval of the perforations is a/2. The source array is configured to excite specific valley states. Phase delays are adjusted to create specific phase windings. Outcoupling fields are measured to determine the momentum of excited states. Far-field radiation patterns are measured to verify directionality. Surface transmission is measured to verify the existence of surface states. Surface field distributions are mapped and Fourier-transformed. The propagation of surface states through sharp corners is measured.

Key Results
The 3D VPC exhibits a complete photonic bandgap when ∆D ≠ 0. The six valleys are grouped pairwise due to time-reversal symmetry. Eigenstates at Wz± display typical vortex profiles with opposite chirality. The Berry curvature at Wz± has nonzero components only in the kx-ky plane. The measured outcoupling fields at 13.8 GHz exhibit different directions. For clockwise phase winding, the direction is −32.9°. For counterclockwise phase winding, the direction is +32.9°. Without phase winding, the direction is 0°, corresponding to X. The radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space. The valley Chern vectors are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The surface transmission maintains high within the complete photonic bandgap. The bulk transmission is substantially lower than the surface transmission. A nearly-linear surface dispersion is observed in the bandgap. The chiral surface states exhibit canalization behavior. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction. The surface states propagate along −z direction on the (010) surface. The surface states propagate along −y direction on the (001) surface. The surface states propagate along +z direction on the (010) surface. The direction of VCVs and circulating direction obey the right-hand-thumb rule. The surface states pass through the sharp corner with high transmission. Only the surface states around the Wx− valley are excited.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys. These valleys are characterized by valley Chern vectors. The vectorial nature enables the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices. It also enables canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and propagation direction are governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. This rule is an intrinsic relation between VCVs and valley surface states. The orbital moments carried by 3D valley states control angular momentum. Highly directional outcoupling can serve as a mechanism for narrow-beam antennae. Robust 2D canalized valley chiral surface states inspire 3D photonic devices. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical ranges.

Contradictions And Limitations
Previous studies were limited to 2D systems. 2D systems suffer from out-of-plane losses. 2D systems can only manipulate light in planar geometries. The complete photonic bandgap was a significant challenge. The study is demonstrated at lower frequencies. The extension to higher frequencies is theoretical.

Claims
The 3D topological valley photonic crystal supports canalized chiral valley surface states on all surfaces. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction. The surface states propagate along −z direction on the (010) surface. The surface states propagate along −y direction on the (001) surface. The surface states propagate along +z direction on the (010) surface.  This enables 3D waveguiding and directional radiation. It allows for the creation of narrow-beam antennae.
The direction of valley surface states is governed by the right-hand-thumb rule relative to the valley Chern vectors. The direction of VCVs and circulating direction obey the right-hand-thumb rule. The right-hand-thumb rule applies to all sample surfaces.  This provides a predictable mechanism for controlling light flow.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The next-nearest neighbor coupling suppresses high-order modes. The boundary condition is tuned by varying D3 and h. The surface states are robust against sharp corners.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the 3D VPC characterized by vectorial Berry curvatures. Figure 2 shows the selective excitation of vectorial valley states. Figure 3 demonstrates the observation of canalized chiral valley surface states. Figure 4 illustrates the right-hand-thumb rule relating surface states with VCVs.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of 3D topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap. 2. The strongest evidence is the experimental demonstration of canalized chiral valley surface states on all surfaces. 3. The future path involves extending the concept to terahertz and optical ranges.
